blocks.text: Viruses are not considered organisms because they are acellular: they are not made of cells. They lack the characteristics of the three domains of life, so they are not classified in any domain or kingdom. A virus consists of nucleic acid, DNA or RNA, surrounded by a protein coat. Viruses cannot run any metabolism of their own; they depend on a host cell, which may be a plant, animal or bacterial cell, to replicate and to synthesise their proteins.

blocks.title: Capsid and the ICTV
blocks.text: The protein coat around a virus's nucleic acid is called the capsid. Viruses are classified by several characteristics, including their genetic material, their replication strategy, their morphology and the hosts they infect. The classification follows guidelines established by the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV).

blocks.title: Prions and viroids
blocks.text: Prions and viroids are also acellular, and they are also not considered living organisms. Prions are composed of protein only. Viroids are composed of circular RNA only. Both kinds of particle cause infectious diseases in certain plants.
Classification on the basis of host range

items: Animal viruses infect animals, including humans. Examples: influenza virus, rabies virus.
Plant viruses infect plants. Examples: tobacco mosaic virus, potato virus X.
Bacteriophages infect bacteria. Examples: T4 phage, lambda phage.
Archaea viruses infect archaea. Example: Sulfolobus spindle-shaped virus.

blocks.text: Classification on the basis of morphology

items: Helical viruses have a capsid with a helical structure wound around the nucleic acid. Examples: tobacco mosaic virus, rabies virus.
Icosahedral viruses have a capsid with a symmetrical icosahedral shape (twenty triangular faces). Examples: adenoviruses, herpesviruses.

Complex viruses have a complex structure, often combining icosahedral and helical features, sometimes with additional structures such as tails. Example: bacteriophages, the viruses that infect bacteria.
Enveloped viruses have an outer lipid envelope, derived from the host cell membrane, surrounding the capsid. Examples: influenza virus, HIV.
Non-enveloped (naked) viruses lack an outer lipid envelope and consist only of a capsid enclosing the nucleic acid. Examples: poliovirus, adenovirus.

blocks.text: Classification on the basis of genetic material

items: DNA viruses have DNA as their genetic material. The DNA can be single-stranded (ssDNA) or double-stranded (dsDNA). dsDNA viruses: adenoviruses (respiratory infections) and herpesviruses (herpes, chickenpox). ssDNA viruses: parvoviruses (gastroenteritis).

RNA viruses have RNA as their genetic material. The RNA can be single-stranded (ssRNA) or double-stranded (dsRNA). ssRNA viruses: coronaviruses (COVID-19) and influenza viruses (flu). dsRNA viruses: rotaviruses (gastroenteritis).

blocks.text: Classification on the basis of replication strategy

items: Positive-sense RNA viruses: the RNA genome is translated directly into proteins by the host cell's ribosomes. Examples: poliovirus, hepatitis C virus.
Negative-sense RNA viruses: the RNA genome is first transcribed into mRNA by a viral RNA polymerase, and only then translated. Examples: rabies virus, Ebola virus.

Reverse-transcribing viruses replicate through a DNA intermediate using the enzyme reverse transcriptase. They can have an RNA or a DNA genome. RNA genome: retroviruses such as HIV, which causes AIDS. DNA genome: hepadnaviruses such as hepatitis B virus.
